lede: The story is that Conor McGregor arrived as a bouncing, wide-stanced karate fighter and left as a flat-footed boxer. We wrote that story down as seven measurable claims, measured every live second of sixteen fights from his body alone, and checked each change against his opponents filmed in the same frames.
answer:
Most of the story doesn't survive the camera, and the part that does is in his upper body. His stance width, knees, guard and shoulders stayed where they were from 2012 to 2021. His bounce faded, but so did his opponents', in the same frames. What changed in him alone, small but consistent: his torso tipped forward, his head came out over his front, and his hips settled back over his rear foot.

And he was never on his toes. Read from his heels directly, he was the flatter-footed fighter in 11 of 14 fights, early and late. The constant across the decade is a long lead hand, held farther out than anyone he fought.

readings.stance_width: His own stance width barely moved (ρ +0.04). His opponents' widened steadily over the decade (ρ +0.80), almost certainly the cameras: UFC broadcasts moved to lower, more side-on angles that show more of a stance. Against that drift he narrowed, the direction the story predicts, but only at p 0.047 before correction (0.28 after).
readings.rear_heel_up: No trend in how high his rear heel sat, alone or against his opponents. The heel index mixes in which way the foot points at the camera, so only the opponent-relative series is meaningful, and it is flat.
readings.bounce: He did bounce less over time (ρ −0.58; −0.66 when the short fights are included). So did his opponents (ρ −0.42), filmed by the same cameras. Relative to them, nothing changed. Whether the cameras smoothed everyone or the division got calmer, it was not a McGregor-specific change.
readings.guard: His hands sat at the same height in 2021 as in 2012, well below his shoulders. If anything his opponents dropped their hands over time, not him.
readings.kicks_per_min: No trend. The kick counter only sees kicks that rise above the standing knee, so calf kicks, which he used heavily late in his career, are invisible to it. This claim is under-measured, not refuted.
readings.switches_per_min: Measured switching rose relative to opponents, the opposite of the prediction and the only result that survives correction. Treat it with care: stance-side reads are right 80–90 % of the time, so even fighters who never switch read one to three switches a minute. His southpaw share stayed near 90 % in every era; he did not become a switcher.
readings.range: The distance he fought at did not trend over his career. It did move within one rivalry: from 2.15 torso lengths against Diaz in March 2016 to 2.41 in the August rematch, the adjustment he was praised for.

overlay_note: Every standing frame from before Diaz 1 (blue) against every frame after (red), fights weighted equally. The two figures nearly coincide: same feet, same hands, same height. The late figure leans slightly further forward over the hips, a change his opponents made too.
instrument_note:
Before reading anything into McGregor's numbers, we checked whether the instrument recovers things already known. Every opponent's fighting stance is public. The pose model, which has never seen these fights, reads the orthodox fighters as orthodox and the southpaws as southpaws.

It is right about 80 to 90 % of the time per frame. That is good enough for shares, and it sets a noise floor for anything built on counting changes of stance.

surprises.title: The long lead hand never changed
surprises.body: In 9 of 11 fights his lead hand sat further out toward the opponent than the opponent's own: 0.57 torso lengths against 0.47 (Wilcoxon p 0.007). That is the measuring, pawing right hand that frames his left. It is the most consistent signature in the data, and it held from Cage Warriors to Poirier.

surprises.title: A slower rhythm than everyone he fought
surprises.body: The dominant frequency of his hip motion was lower than his opponent's in 9 of 11 fights (1.21 against 1.39 bounces a second), and it slowed through his career (ρ −0.72). Not less movement so much as a slower, more deliberate beat.

surprises.title: He leaned in, and so did they
surprises.body: His torso leaned further over his hips toward the opponent as the years went on (ρ +0.65), and his head sat further forward (ρ +0.73). It looks like the boxer's posture the story describes, but his opponents moved the same way, so the measurements can't separate him from the era.

surprises.title: Diaz 2 is visible in the numbers
surprises.body: Against Nate Diaz in August 2016 he stood farther away than in March (2.41 against 2.15 torso lengths, intervals barely overlapping) and leaned further forward over his hips (2.9° against 0.2°). That is the kind of change this instrument can see, which makes its silence on the career-long claims more meaningful.

method:
1. Every fight with a public upload. Sixteen videos, official UFC, UFC Fight Pass or broadcaster uploads where they exist, two fan uploads where none do, at most 720p.
  2. Live play only. The fight clock is found automatically in each broadcast: the overlay whose edges stay at the same pixels while two fighters are on screen. Frames without it (walkouts, replays, interviews, slow motion) are dropped.
  3. Pose, 10 times a second. A UFC-trained fighter detector finds the fighters; RTMW-x places 133 points on each, including both feet. No model was trained or tuned for this study.
  4. Who is who. Shorts colour, with each fight's two colours named by eye once from sample crops. Inside a camera shot, a fighter keeps his identity through occlusion by continuity.
  5. Standing only. Both fighters upright, torsos within 45° of vertical, hips more than a torso length apart. Clinch and ground are excluded.
  6. Body units. Every length is divided by the fighter's own torso length in that shot, so zoom cancels. The opponent is measured in the same frames as the control for camera angle and era.
  7. Tests. One number per fight, 95 % intervals by resampling 10-second blocks, rank correlation with fight date, permutation p, Holm correction across the seven claims. Fights with under 60 seconds of standing footage are shown but not tested.
fool:
• Camera angle. Ratios cancel zoom, not angle. That is why every headline number is McGregor minus his opponent in the same frames, and why two of his apparent changes turned out to be shared.
  • Few fights. Eleven fights enter the tests. A real but modest change could hide under that; the narrowing stance (p 0.047 before correction) may be one.
  • Short fights. Aldo (13 s, replays only), Cerrone and O'Keeffe (13 and 9 s standing) can't say much. Rerunning with a 30-second minimum, or with official uploads only, keeps every claim's direction; stance switching is the only result that survives correction in all three runs, and the narrowing stance weakens when the short fights are added (ρ −0.38).
  • What counts as a kick. Only kicks that rise above the standing knee; low calf kicks are missed. About three in four counted kicks were real kicks or knees when checked by eye.
  • Model reviewed, not expert labelled. Points come from an off-the-shelf model checked by eye on samples (feet, kicks, stances), not hand-labelled.
closing: Ghost Fight lab · pose from RTMW-x and a UFC-trained detector, no training · after Peter Wang's deep-sports-analysis · code and pre-registration in mma/study/mcgregor
stance_read:
What the skeleton supports. Over his career McGregor's torso tipped further toward his opponent (about 1° to 3.5° of lean, ρ +0.68) and his head came further out over his front (ρ +0.64), while his hips settled slightly back over his rear foot (ρ −0.62). All three hold when only side-on shots are used, and his opponents, filmed by the same cameras, show no clear trend in any of them. That is a real, if small, change in posture: the upper body loaded forward over a base that stayed back. A coiled counter-puncher's shape more than a walk-forward boxer's.

What it doesn't. His feet never narrowed: the opponents' stances "widened" over the decade instead, which is the cameras. His knees, crouch and guard height didn't move. His shoulders didn't hunch. His bounce did fade, but so did his opponents', in the same frames. And relative to the men across from him he moved more late in his career, not less (ρ +0.68), because they slowed down more than he did.

How sure. Fifteen measures, eleven to fourteen fights each. The three posture changes are each p < 0.03 on their own, which is suggestive, not proof: none would survive a correction for fifteen tests. The changes are also small, a couple of degrees and a few hundredths of a torso length. The morph above needs exaggerating to be seen, and that is the honest scale of it.
feet_read:
He was never on his toes. This is the surprise. The story says he started light on the balls of his feet and became flat-footed. Read from his heels and toes directly, his heels sat lower than his opponent's in 11 of 14 fights (median lift 0.17 of a foot length, against about 0.27 for them), and that didn't change from 2012 to 2021. His ankles also bounced less than his opponents' in 10 of 14 fights. The bounce people remember is real (the hips and shoulders, above), but it rode on flat, quiet feet.

What did change at the feet: the time with both feet planted, heels down and still, roughly doubled, from about 4 % of his standing time to about 7.5 % (ρ +0.60, p 0.026; opponents no clear trend). Still a man in motion almost all the time, but one who settled into his base more often.

Heel lift mixes in which way the foot points at the camera, so the comparison that matters is against the opponent in the same frames, which is the one quoted. Crops below show the tracked ankle (white), heel (red) and big toe (cyan) on random standing frames, so you can judge the points yourself.
